I can give it unquali- fied recommendation." 25c, 50c $1 at Alvey & List and G. C. C. Kolb's drug stores. ENGINE TEST. Big Locomotive Could Not Pull Train Over Iron Ore Hill.
The first test of the big freight sent here for trial on the Paducah and Louisville districts of the I. C. was not so satisfactory as it was thought it would be, the engine being unable to take the 1,300 ton train over Iron Ore Hill without "doubling."

She took the other hills all right but bucked at Iron Ore which is one of the highest grade hills on the division. The big engine has not been thoroughly "limbered" up yet and the traveling engineer and master mechanic are looking after her rather closely.

Today the engine was started out again with a 1,100 ton train and will test Scottsburg and Underwood hills this side of Cedar Bluff. Supt. A. H. Egan, of the Louisville division, went up with the train in his private car.
After the engine has been tested on the grades between Paducah and Central City, she will be taken to the Louisville district to test between Central City and Louisville.
ed-mcgaughey-pembroke-1905-08-17.A2:
WHITE BRAKEMAN SHOT Negro Who Did the Shooting Escapes and Others Arrested.
The people of Pembroke were on their metal early in the morning last Thursday. Something like 25 of them armed themselves and were out for gore when the news spread that another white man had been shot by a negro. They have not forgotten the "justice" meted out to the negroes implicated in the murder of an unknown white man within a mile of the city a year ago last November, and woe be to the one who commits a like offense and falls into their hands. It is thought there will be no use for lawyers, judge or jury then. They did all they could to have the more guilty negroes given the same penalty that George Holland suffered, but technicalities of the law cheated them.

Thursday morning five negroes—Johnny Campbell, better known as "Bad Eye," Ed McGaughey, Geo. McKinly, John Henry Houston and another negro whose name has not yet been ascertained, boarded a coal car of train No. 57 at Hopkinsville going south for the purpose of beating their way to the Guthrie fair. When the train had gotten a mile beyond Casky Ed Haynes, a brakeman on 57, discovered them on a coal car and ordered them to get off, and on their refusal to do so Haynes undertook to eject them. Haynes, who was seen by a representative of this paper, as he passed here on his way to his home at Howell, Ind., said that neither of the four negroes who were drawn up in line on the platform for identification when he reached here on the 9:42 train Thursday morning was the man who shot him. He described the negro as being rather heavy, full faced, well dressed and sporting a flying white necktie. He thinks the pistol was a No. 44. After shooting Haynes, he told the other four negroes to get off the train, which they did, and all took to the woods.

The conductor of train No. 57 communicated with Sheriff Lem Davis, who with Capt. Sol Fritz, at the head of the L. & N. detective force on this section, and Booth Morris, Lieutenant of the local police force, took a fast freight, and when near Pembroke found that the Marshal of Pembroke, Joe Jackson, and a posse of citizens had arrested the four negroes and were holding them to be taken charge of by the sheriff. They were turned over to the sheriff and brought here for further developments. "Bad Eye" had received a shot in the back fired from the train, which will incapacitate him from doing anything for some time. The whole lot, it is said, have an unsavory reputation.

Thursday morning they were brought before City Judge Knight on the charge of jumping on a moving train. A fine of $20 each was assessed against Campbell and Houston, and in default of payment they were sent to the work house. The other negroes will be tried today.

Brakeman Haynes received a flesh wound in his left arm, but the one in his right arm is a little more serious, the ball cutting the muscles above the elbow. "Bad Eye"Campbell is a tough character and is well known to the police.

Every effort will be made to find the negro who shot Haynes, and when the detective force of this city and the L. & N. find his trail he will no doubt be run down.

Petitions asking for an election upon the question as to whether or not stock of all kinds will be prohibited from running at large in McCracken county were filed in the county court and probably will be taken up at the next meeting of the fiscal court. The fiscal court has recently called for an election on the hog law and an effort will be made to have the election for a general stock law.

BLOOD POISON
May Result From Wounds Received by Brakeman.
The Evansville Courier says that A. J. Haney, who was shot in both arms near Casky last week by one of the five negroes who were attempting to steal a ride on a freight train, has shown indications of blood poison.
